structures.note: Replaced an original beacon on a small wooden building; now a metal pole with a daymark placard and a solar-powered light (LighthouseFriends; Lighthouse Directory 8 m (26 ft) post)

access.note: Coast Guard property. Grounds and tower closed (LighthouseFriends). The light can be seen from the breakwater.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: LighthouseFriends describes a first beacon at the end of the breakwater in 1924 and the Bureau's second light in 1925. The record's 1925 date matches the second light, the one this record describes; the 1924 beacon is kept as a separate event.

LighthouseFriends places the first navigational light at the end of the breakwater in 1924 and does not date the breakwater itself. The Images of Old Hawaii account gives 1923 to 1926 for the development of the harbor. The two describe different steps and do not contradict each other.

notes_for_editor: (1) Thin station: two secondary sources (LighthouseFriends, the Directory) and one local history site. The Lighthouse Service Bulletins 1913-1939 do not name the light under the OCR spellings tried (Kaumalapau, Kaumalapa, Lanai, Lanai Island). (2) The 1913 and 1914 Bulletin entries that OCR as 'Kanai Island, Hawaii' (a second-order light; a 30 ft steel skeleton tower with a fog-signal station at 116 ft focal plane) appear to be Kauai (Kilauea Point), not Lanai. Not used. (3) No USLHS place record or light-station report for Kaumalapau appears in the USLHS Hawaii list (state_light_station_reports.php?id=11). (4) The record's status note says the coordinates came from OSM; LighthouseFriends' 20.7833, -156.99162 agrees. (5) The Coast Guard Historian's index lists 'Kaumalapau (HI)', but the index page has no article links, so the article could not be reached. (6) mapofus.org describes a 'modest concrete tower', which conflicts with the metal post in LighthouseFriends and the Directory; not used. (7) The USACE Honolulu District page and an ASCE abstract on the breakwater both returned 403 and were not read. (8) Love Dean, The Lighthouses of Hawai'i (1986), is the reference LighthouseFriends cites; not read. (9) LighthouseFriends says the first light (1924) was at the breakwater end; the Directory gives only the 1925 station date. (10) The Images of Old Hawaii page quotes a 1926 publication on the breakwater's size; that quotation is secondhand and is not used. (11) Possible follow-up: the Coast Guard's own Lanai page or Honolulu newspapers 1924-1926 for the breakwater and light dates (the one Chronicling America search for 'Kaumalapau' 1922-1930 returned nothing relevant). (12) Checked 2026-10-28: the Coast Guard ownership and the closed grounds and tower rest on LighthouseFriends alone; the Directory gives the site status as unknown, and the story says so. The breakwater is placed on its north side ('by constructing a breakwater on the north side of this small indentation'), not across the gulch mouth as the earlier draft said. The 'concrete jacks (tetrapods)' wording is LighthouseFriends' own.
